content: The Carnegie Institution for Science, also known as the Carnegie Institution of Washington (CIW), is a U.S.-based organization established to advance scientific research. It focuses on six primary areas of study: plant molecular biology at the Department of Plant Biology in Stanford, California; developmental biology at the Department of Embryology in Baltimore, Maryland; global ecology at the Department of Global Ecology in Stanford, California; earth science, materials science, and astrobiology at the Geophysical Laboratory in Washington, D.C.; earth and planetary sciences, as well as astronomy, at the Department of Terrestrial Magnetism in Washington, D.C.; and astronomy at the Observatories of the Carnegie Institution of Washington, located in Pasadena, California, and Las Campanas, Chile. The Carnegie Institution was founded in 1902 by Andrew Carnegie, who envisioned it as a unique organization dedicated to scientific discovery in the broadest and most liberal sense. Its mission has been to support exceptional individuals who can explore complex scientific problems with complete freedom. This guiding principle, established by Carnegie and his trustees, has allowed the institution to maintain flexibility and independence, which are essential for its success. The institution continues to support research in earth, space, and life sciences. Andrew Carnegie, beginning in 1895, donated his vast fortune to establish 23 organizations worldwide, which today bear his name and work in diverse fields such as art, education, international affairs, world peace, and scientific research. These organizations are independent entities, related only by name. In 2007, the institution adopted the name Carnegie Institution for Science to better distinguish itself from other Carnegie organizations and to emphasize its focus on science. Legally, it remains the Carnegie Institution of Washington but now has a public identity that more clearly reflects its work. The institution has a long history of supporting groundbreaking research. For example, it provided a grant to George Hale in 1904, which was used to construct the 60-inch Hale Telescope on Mount Wilson in California. This was followed by the design and construction of the 100-inch Hooker Telescope, completed in 1917, and later the 200-inch telescope at the Palomar Observatory, partially funded by a Rockefeller grant. The institution also supports the operation of the 5-meter Magellan Telescopes, which have over four times the light-gathering capacity of existing instruments. In the field of genetics, the Carnegie Institution merged the Eugenics Record Office with the Station for Experimental Evolution in 1920 to form its Department of Genetics. This department was funded until 1939, and its records were preserved in a university library after its closure in 1944. The institution continues to support genetic research, with notable grantees including Nobel laureates Barbara McClintock, Alfred Hershey, and Andrew Fire. The institution has also contributed to archaeological research, particularly in the Yucatán Peninsula, from the 1910s to the 1930s. It supported extensive excavations of pre-Columbian Maya civilization sites, including Chichen Itza and Copán, under the leadership of Carnegie associate and Mayanist scholar Sylvanus G. Morley. The Carnegie Institution has been led by several distinguished presidents, including Daniel Coit Gilman (1902–1904), Robert S. Woodward (1904–1920), John C. Merriam (1921–1938), Vannevar Bush (1939–1955), Caryl P. Haskins (1956–1971), Philip Abelson (1971–1978), James D. Ebert (1978–1987), Edward E. David, Jr. (acting president, 1987–1988), Maxine F. Singer (1989–2002), and others.
